title: How the Rolling Jubilee Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the Rolling Jubilee, a project of Strike Debt (an offshoot of Occupy Wall Street) that buys portfolios of delinquent consumer debt cheaply and forgives it. They cover the consumer debt problem in the US, how the secondary debt market arose from savings and loan crisis-era write-off rules, how debt portfolios are bought and sold for pennies on the dollar, the biblical Jubilee origin in Leviticus, critiques of the model (including the Corinthian Colleges student debt purchase), and the tax question. The episode opens with a Movie Crush guest request from Chuck and ends with listener mail thanking fans for gifts.

segments.title: Movie Crush guest call and opening banter
segments.summary: Chuck promotes his new solo podcast Movie Crush and asks for guests. Hosts open the episode introducing the Rolling Jubilee and the topic of consumer debt.

segments.title: US consumer debt and delinquent debt statistics
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the size of US household debt, citing figures from different years, and the share that is delinquent. They distinguish good debt from bad debt and describe how lenders pass delinquent accounts to collection agencies.

segments.title: Selling debt and the Occupy origins of the Rolling Jubilee
segments.summary: Lenders sell delinquent debt to investors, and the hosts compare this to the mortgage crisis. They explain that the Rolling Jubilee buys debt to forgive it, and that it grew out of Occupy Wall Street through Thomas Gorkin and Strike Debt, framed as a bailout for consumers.

segments.title: Structure of Rolling Jubilee and volunteers
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Rolling Jubilee's board, unpaid volunteers, and a few paid brokers and web developers paid below market rate.

segments.title: Origins of the word jubilee in Leviticus
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck trace the word jubilee to the Hebrew yobel, meaning ram's horn, and the Book of Leviticus, which calls for debts to be forgiven and land returned every fifty years. They note ancient debt-forgiveness traditions in Babylonia, Egypt, and the Rosetta Stone.

segments.title: How debt portfolios are bought and sold
segments.summary: After the savings and loan crisis, banks were required to write off delinquent accounts after 90 days and could take a tax deduction, creating the secondary consumer debt market. Banks bundle written-off debt into portfolios sold for pennies on the dollar, and buyers collect partial settlements, sometimes at about 50 cents on the dollar, and make profits. An example given is Encore Capital Group spending $47 million on $1.1 billion of debt.

segments.title: Critiques of debt collection and how Rolling Jubilee acquires debt
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the unfairness of targeting vulnerable debtors and the way the Rolling Jubilee cannot be asked to buy a specific person's debt. It buys portfolios, forgives them, and sometimes contacts debtors, who often treat the letters as scams. Forgiveness happens regardless of donation. The hosts note the goal is awareness.

segments.title: Sheep's clothing strategy, Corinthian Colleges, and tax questions
segments.summary: Strike Debt initially planned to buy debt through intermediaries, but found the industry willing to sell. The hosts discuss brokers and online portfolio sites, the Corinthian Colleges student debt purchase, and criticism that buying debt funds the industry. A legal opinion held that forgiven debt is not taxable income. Figures given: about $32 million forgiven and roughly $700,000 raised at the time.

segments.title: Wrap-up of Rolling Jubilee discussion
segments.summary: The hosts conclude that the Rolling Jubilee is a small but awareness-raising effort, and mention a possible future episode on debt, debt collection, and bankruptcy.

segments.title: Listener mail and gifts
segments.summary: Chuck reads thank-you notes and lists gifts from listeners, including patches, postcards, copper flasks, candy, chips, hot sauce, paintings, and books. Josh gives social media and contact information and signs off.
